APPLICATION FOR MINOR VARIANCE
TO: Township of Norwich Committee of Adjustment
MEETING: October 14, 2025
REPORT NUMBER: CP 2025-292
OWNERS: Richard and Ramona Schveighardt
793424 Slant Road, Norwich, ON N0J 1P0
VARIANCE REQUESTED:
1. Table 5.1.1.3 – Lot Coverage for Accessory Structures, to increase the permitted lot
coverage from 170 m2 (1,830 ft2) to 263 m2 (2,831 ft2) to recognize a recently constructed
accessory structure and maintain an existing detached accessory structure on the subject
lands.
VARIANCE RECOMMENDED:
1. Table 5.1.1.3 – Lot Coverage for Accessory Structures, to increase the permitted lot
coverage from 170 m2 (1,830 ft2) to 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) to recognize a recently constructed
accessory structure and maintain an existing detached accessory structure on the subject
lands.
LOCATION:
The subject lands are described as Part of Lot 6, Concession 3 (North Norwich), in the Township
of Norwich. The subject lands are located on the east side of Slant Road lying between Quaker
Street and Evergreen Street and are municipally known as 793424 Slant Road.
BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
COUNTY OF OXFORD OFFICIAL PLAN:
Schedule ‘N-1’ Township of Norwich Land Use Plan Agricultural Reserve
TOWNSHIP OF NORWICH ZONING BY-LAW: Residential Existing Lot Zone (RE)
File Number: A21-25 Report Number 2025-292
Page 2
SURROUNDING USES:
Predominantly agricultural with a number of non-farm rural residential parcels of varying sizes in
the immediate vicinity.
COMMENTS:
(a) Purpose of the Application:
The applicants are proposing relief from the above-noted provisions of the Township Zoning By-
law to recognize a recently constructed accessory building (approximately 167.2 m2 (1,800 ft2) in
size) and an existing barn that is used for storage (approximately 72.8 m2 (784 ft2) in size). The
total gross floor area of all accessory structures is approximately 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) in size,
whereas 170 m2 (1,830 ft2) is permitted in the ‘Residential Existing Zone (RE)’.
Initially, the applicants had agreed to demolish the existing barn structure when the new
accessory building was completed. However, through discussion with the applicants they would
prefer to maintain both structures for personal storage and it was noted that the subject minor
variance would be required.
While the application submitted for the variances requesting a total gross floor area of 263 m2
(2,831 ft2), reviewing the sketch submitted by the applicant, the coverage results in a total of
240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) and the report will recommend this amended relief to align with the applicants’
drawing.
The subject lands do contain a portion of non-ecologically important woodlands identified in the
Oxford Natural Heritage Systems Study (ONHSS); however, the recently constructed accessory
building is already located within this area and was situated in a way that there was little impact
from the development.
The subject property comprises an area of approximately 0.94 ha (2.32 ac) and currently contains
a single detached dwelling with attached garage, the existing barn and the recently constructed
accessory building.
Plate 1, Location Map with Existing Zoning, shows the location of the subject lands and the current
zoning in the immediate vicinity.
Plate 2, Subject Lands (2020 Aerial Photo), provides an aerial view of the subject lands.
Plate 3, Applicants’ Sketch, identifies the location of the existing structures and the proposed
accessory structure on the subject lands, as well as their setbacks and dimensions.
(b) Agency Comments
The Township of Norwich Fire Department and County of Oxford Public Works have indicated
that they have no objections to the proposal.
Township of Norwich Building Department confirmed that the location of the new accessory
building was located the required distance from the municipal drain as per the zoning by-law and
was inspected at time of footing installation.
File Number: A21-25 Report Number 2025-292
Page 3
(c) Public Consultation
Public Notice was provided to surrounding property owners on September 17, 2025, in
accordance with the provisions of the Planning Act. At the time of writing this report, no comments
or concerns had been received from the public.
(d) Intent and Purpose of the Official Plan:
The subject property is located within the Agricultural Reserve designation according to the
Official Plan, which supports a wide range of agricultural type land uses. The Official Plan also
recognizes existing non-farm rural residential uses, together with their accessory buildings on
lands designated as Agricultural Reserve and it is the intent of the Official Plan to ensure that
non-farm rural residential uses shall not hinder surrounding agricultural operations.
Planning staff are generally satisfied that the development of a residential accessory structure will
have minimal impact on surrounding agricultural land uses. As such, staff are of the opinion that
the requested variances are in-keeping with the intent of the Official Plan.
(e) Intent and Purpose of the Zoning By-law:
The subject property is zoned ‘Residential Existing Lot Zone (RE)’, which permits single detached
dwellings and accessory structures thereto.
Accessory structures are permitted on parcels zoned ‘RE’ to a maximum lot coverage of
170 m2 (1,830 ft²) of gross floor area or 10% of the lot area, whichever is lesser. This provision
is intended to ensure such structures remain clearly secondary and ancillary to the main use of
the property and limit impacts on neighbouring properties. This provision also assists to ensure
sufficient space is maintained on the property to accommodate private services, grading/drainage
and amenity space.
In this case, the applicants have recently constructed a new accessory building being
approximately 167.2 m2 (1,800 ft2) but also want to maintain an existing barn structure being
approximately 72.8 m2 (784 ft2), that is being used for personal storage as well. The applicants
had indicated that they would demolish the barn structure after the new building was constructed,
however, the applicants have now submitted the subject application in order to keep both
structures with an increased total lot coverage for all accessory buildings.
Planning staff are satisfied that the subject lands are of sufficient size to provide adequate space
to accommodate the recently constructed accessory structure and existing barn, and given the
proposed location, being setback sufficiently from Slant Road, as well as being located within the
rear yard on the property, staff are satisfied that the proposed accessory structure will remain
secondary and ancillary to the main residential use of the property, provide for all other applicable
setbacks required by the zoning by-law, and provide for amenity space and adequate area for the
provision of private services.
(f) Desirable Development/Use:
The applicants have requested the above noted relief to recognize a recently constructed
accessory structure and an existing barn structure which results in a cumulative overall gross floor
area of 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) for all accessory structures whereas the Zoning By-law permits 170 m2
(1,830 ft2).

Staff are of the opinion that the proposed development will be in-keeping with the general
characteristics of existing development in the immediate area and will have minimal impact on
surrounding land uses. Staff are satisfied that the requested relief to increase the cumulative
gross floor of accessory structures to 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) is appropriate given that the subject
property, at approximately 2.32 ac (0.94 ha), is much larger than the required lot area for rural
residential properties. Further, while the gross floor area of the proposed building is larger, the
proposal equates to a total of 2.5% cumulative lot coverage of the existing and proposed detached
accessory structures.
Staff are further satisfied that there will be no negative impacts on surrounding property owners.
No comments of concern were received from the neighbours. In light of the foregoing, it is the
opinion of this Office that the requested relief meets the four tests of a minor variance.
RECOMMENDATION:
That the … Committee of Adjustment approve Application File A21-25, submitted by Rick and
Ramona Schveighardt for lands described as Part of Lot 6, Concession 3 (North Norwich), in the
Township of Norwich, as it relates to:
1. Table 5.1.1.3 – Lot Coverage for Accessory Structures, to increase the permitted lot
coverage from 170 m2 (1,830 ft2) to 263 m2 (2,590 ft2) to recognize a recently constructed
accessory structure and maintain an existing detached accessory structure on the subject
lands.

VARIANCE REQUESTED:
1. Relief from Section 11.2, R1 Zone provisions, to reduce the required interior side yard
width from 1.5 m (4.9 ft) to 0.94 m (3.11 ft) to recognize an existing deficient side yard
width to facilitate the construction of a two-storey dwelling.
LOCATION:
The subject lands are described as Lot 11, North side of Main Street, Plan 43, in the Township of
Norwich. The lands are located on the north side of Main Street lying between Grove Street and
Maple Street and are municipally known as 276 Main Street West, Village of Otterville.

SURROUNDING USES:
Surrounding land uses include low density residential type housing in the village of Otterville. Otter
Creek is located to the east, and the Otter Creek golf course is located to the south of the subject
lands.
COMMENTS:
(a) Purpose of the Application:
The applicant is seeking relief from the Township Zoning By-law in order to recognize an existing
legal non-conforming interior side yard width of 0.94 m (3.11 ft). The subject lands previously
contained a one storey dwelling which benefitted from a lesser interior side yard based on the
zoning provisions of previous versions of the zoning by-law. The previous dwelling was recently
razed by fire and the applicants are proposing to replace the dwelling, on the same foundation,
with a two storey dwelling.
Section 5.19.6 of the Zoning By-law does recognize the ability for additions to non-conforming
buildings, provided that the addition does not contravene any other zoning provisions. In this
instance, the addition will contravene the interior side yard setback provisions and therefore the
variance is required to recognize the deficiency.
The subject lands are approximately 1,057.68 m2 (11,386.7 ft2) in area, are currently vacant aside
from the foundation of the previous dwelling. A two storey dwelling is proposed and a detached
garage.
Plate 1, Location Map with Existing Zoning, shows the location of the subject lands and the current
zoning in the immediate vicinity.
Plate 2, Aerial Map (2020), shows the location of the subject lands and surrounding properties,
and the location of the existing bunker silos.
Plate 3, Applicant’s Sketch, illustrates the subject lands and the proposed silo.
(b) Agency Comments
Township of Norwich Fire Department and Oxford County Public Works indicated no concerns
with the subject application.
Township of Norwich Building Department noted that a Real Property Report will be required to
confirm that setback and location of the foundation as it exists.
(c) Public Consultation:
The application was circulated on September 25, 2025, in accordance with the requirements of
the Planning Act. To date, no concerns or objections with the application have been raised.
(d) Intent and Purpose of the Official Plan:
The subject property is located within the Village of Otterville, which is designated ‘Village’
according to the Settlement Strategy Plan for the County of Oxford, and ‘Settlement’ according to
the Township of Norwich Land Use Plan. Within these designations, a range of land uses are
permitted, with the exception of multiple unit residential development involving more than two
units.

Planning staff are generally satisfied that the construction of single detached dwelling is in keeping
with the Settlement policies of Official Plan.
(e) Intent and Purpose of the Zoning By-law:
The subject lands are currently zoned ‘Residential Type 1 Zone (R1)’, according to the Township
of Norwich Zoning By-law. Permitted uses within the R1 zone include a single detached dwelling,
home occupation, a group home, and accessory buildings/structures.
The provisions of the R1 zone require a minimum lot area of 2,800 m2 (30,140 ft2) where sanitary
sewers are not available, minimum lot depth of 50 m (164 ft), front yard depth of 7.5 m (24.6 ft),
rear yard depth of 7.5 m (24.6 ft), exterior side yard width of 7.5 m (24.6 ft) and an interior side
yard width of 1.5 m (4.9 ft). Properties within the R1 zone are permitted a maximum lot coverage
of 30%.
The existing foundation has an approximate interior side yard setback of 0.94 m (3.11 ft), the
previous version of the zoning by-law (1976) permitted an interior side yard of 1.2 m (4 ft) which
is why the foundation exists as it does. The previous one storey dwelling would have benefitted
from a legal non-conforming status when the current zoning by-law (2003) was passed. When the
existing dwelling was razed by fire, it could have been replaced by another one storey dwelling,
however, the applicants are proposing a two storey dwelling instead.
As noted, Section 5.19.6 does permit the extension or addition to a non-conforming use, building
or structure, provided that the extension or addition does not contravene any of the zone
provisions of the Zoning By-law. As the applicants are proposing a two storey dwelling, the
addition of another storey is contravening the zoning provisions, specifically the required interior
side yard width.
Side yard width provisions are intended to ensure that there is adequate space for the
maintenance of the property, proper drainage, and appropriate access to the remainder of the
property. The applicant is proposing a setback of 0.94 m (3.11 ft) which would recognize the
location of the existing foundation. Staff are satisfied that the proposed setback is sufficient to
allow for access around the dwelling and for drainage and maintenance purposes.
(f) Desirable Development/Use:
The application for minor variance has been requested to facilitate the construction of a two storey
dwelling in place of a one storey razed by fire.
Staff are satisfied that the proposed interior side yard setback will recognize an existing legal non-
conforming foundation and permit an additional storey to be constructed.
In light of the foregoing, Planning staff are of the opinion that the requested variance can be
considered to be minor in nature, desirable for the appropriate development and use of the land
and in-keeping with the general intent and purpose of the Zoning By-law and the objectives and
policies of the Official Plan with respect to accessory structures.

1.2 County of Oxford Growth Forecast Area Municipal and
Settlement Area Allocations
Building on the County-wide forecasts provided in Section 1.1, population, housing, and
employment allocations by Area Municipality were developed. These allocations have
been based on a detailed review of the following local supply and demand factors:
Local Supply Factors
• Supply of potential future housing stock in the development approvals process by
housing structure type, approval status, and location;
• Current inventory of net vacant designated “greenfield” lands not currently in the
development approvals process;
• Residential intensification opportunities;
• Supply of designated vacant Employment Area lands by Area Municipality;
• Consideration of water and wastewater servicing capacity; and
• Provincial, County, and Area Municipal policy direction regarding forecast
residential growth by Settlement Area and Rural Area.
Demand Factors
• Historical population, housing, and employment trends based on Statistics
Canada (Census) data by Area Municipality;
• A review of recent residential and non-residential building permit data by housing
structure type and employment sector by Area Municipality;
• Historical commuting trends and anticipated employment growth opportunities
within the surrounding market area;
• A review of local employment opportunities by sector and Area Municipality.
• Forecast population trends by major age group and associated household
formation trends by age of household maintainer;
• Consideration of long-term housing needs by housing tenure (i.e. ownership vs.
rental housing) and influence on housing demand by structure type; and
• Housing market demand by Area Municipality across all major demographic
groups, including young adults, new families, move-up buyers, and empty
nesters/seniors.

Oxford County 2024 - Growth Analysis and Land Needs Assessment Package - September 10 2025
While population and employment growth rates vary significantly by geographic area,
each of the Area Municipalities within the County share several common attributes with
respect to near- and longer-term population growth and development trends. These
include the following:
• All Area Municipalities are forecast to experience higher total annual population
housing and employment growth relative to historical trends experienced
between 2011 and 2021.
• Continued regional employment opportunities, particularly those related to
manufacturing; goods movement; agricultural; as well other service-producing
and knowledge-based sectors, represent a key driver of future employment
growth within the County and its Area Municipalities.
• Declining housing affordability, combined with a range of broader economic
headwinds, including persistently high inflation rates, rising household debt, U.S.
protectionist policy, and a slower short-term economic outlook at the national,
provincial and regional level are anticipated to dampen housing demand in the
near term (i.e., next 12 to 24 months), relative to recent historical highs
experienced during the past five years.
• Over the longer term (i.e., 10+ years), the average rate of annual housing
development is anticipated to gradually slow (relative the medium-term forecast
period i.e. next decade) across all Area Municipalities within the County, driven
by modestly slower regional and provincial economic growth associated with an
aging population and regional labour force.
• Low-density housing forms are forecast comprise a notable share of future
housing growth; however, increasing market demand will exist for medium- and
high-density housing types across all Area Municipalities.

Public Participation in Electronic Council Meetings and Planning Public Meetings/
Hearings Protocol
Please note: That, in order to reduce strain on the technology, if you only wish to listen to the
meeting please access the livestream on the Township’s YouTube Channel
Purpose:
This procedure has been created to establish a protocol for public participation in electronic
Council and Planning Public Meetings in the Township of Oro-Medonte in accordance with
Section 238 (3.3) of the Municipal Act, 2001, the Planning Act, 1990, c.P.13. and the
Emergency Management and Civil Protection Act. This procedure also outlines the public
responsibility in order to participate in an electronic meeting via telephone or video.
Scope:
The procedure applies to all members of the public, applicants, consultants and delegates
wishing to participate in an electronic Council or Planning Public Meeting, either via video or
telephone. Nevertheless, this policy is subject to rules of procedure as stated in the
Procedural By-law and other Provincial legislation.
Definitions:
Electronic Meeting – a meeting hosted through telephone conference call or video platform
Video Conferencing Solutions – an electronic meeting platform
Chair – Mayor or Designate
Members – Members of Council
Clerk/Designate – means the Clerk of the Township of Oro-Medonte, or Deputy Clerk, acting
in the capacity of the Clerk in his/her absence, or a person who the Clerk has delegated
authority to in accordance with Section 228(4) of the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended.
IT – Information Technology Division
Share Screen Viewing – two or more applications visible on screen at once (eg. Power Point
Presentation and participating Members)
Waiting Room – a virtual room where attendees wait to join the meeting or are placed in, in
the event of a pecuniary interest
Page 1 of 6
Procedure:
Open Forum
Public attendance to Electronic Meetings during the course of an Emergency may be
restricted to electronic means and will be indicated on the meeting agenda.
There are two ways you can participate in Open Forum during a Council Meeting - by
Electronic Participation or Written Submissions.
Electronic Participation (speaking during Open Forum using ZOOM):
• If you wish to make an oral statement during the Open Forum portion of a Council
Meeting on an agenda item, please submit a completed Request for Public
Participation Form, found on the Township website, prior to noon on Monday before the
meeting to register or call 705-487-2171.
• Ensure you have a device with internet access to participate electronically as an
‘Attendee’ to make your oral statement during the meeting. Please refer to following
tutorial for ZOOM details: https://support.zoom.us/hc/en-us/categories/200101697
• While computer attendance is encouraged, if you do not have the necessary
technology to participate by computer, you may use a telephone and call in to make
your Open Forum comments. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person; registration
is still required to present Open Forum comments.
• If you are participating by telephone, you will not have the option to type in your name.
We will ask for the phone number you will be using to participate in the meeting. This
information will let us associate the correct name with your phone number. Please
note, that depending on the volume of speakers, telephone numbers may be visible to
the public; however, every effort will be made to change prior to attendees being
promoted to panelists.
• Once you have completed the Request for Public Participation Form regarding a
Council meeting agenda item and the webinar registration is closed, all applicants are
uploaded to ZOOM. Meeting invites are then sent by Zoom to the e-mail you provided
in the registration form.
• Please note this link is unique to you and should not be shared with others. Only those
whose registration form was received will be permitted attendance.
On the day of the meeting, we ask that you join the meeting fifteen to twenty (15-20)
minutes before your scheduled time to speak. When joining via ZOOM, please type in
your name so we know who you are. You will be granted the ability to unmute your
microphone when it is your time to speak. Please wait for the Chair to request you to
speak. You will be able to hear and view the meeting in progress. You will not be able
to see other attendees nor will you appear on video
Page 2 of 6
• When you have finished speaking, unless you anticipate making further comments, we
ask that you leave the Zoom Meeting. If you wish to follow the meeting, please watch
it on the Township’s YouTube Channel. If you do not leave the meeting and have to
be removed by the host, you will not be able to return to the meeting.
• Please do not watch the livestream on YouTube while you are using the ZOOM
technology as this can distort the sound.
Written submissions submitted by email
• Depending on circumstances, an Electronic Meeting may not permit an in-person
Open Forum, but will permit electronic submissions received in advance of the
meeting.
• Agenda Comment input shall be submitted through an email containing your name,
address and your comments regarding the agenda item to agendacomment@oro-
medonte.ca by 3:00 p.m. the day prior to the start of the Electronic Meeting, or as
otherwise noted on the agenda. Your correspondence will be directed in accordance
with the amended procedural by-law and filed with the Township as part of the public
record.
As noted above, your comments must relate to an item on the agenda. Please note you are
free to contact any member of Council directly with other matters or questions at
council@oro-medonte.ca or via telephone at the following link Contact Us.
For all meetings, the Clerk/designate will authorize all requests to ensure they are related to
agenda items for the meeting.
The Corporate Services Division will ensure that information on how the public may access
and provide input during the meeting is provided on the meeting agenda and on the
Township website.
Deputations and Presentations
• Submit a completed Request for Public Participation Form found on the Township
website, including preferred meeting date.
• Ensure any presentation material you wish to share during your deputation is received
by the Clerk by 9:00 a.m. 10 calendar days prior to the preferred meeting.
• All presentation material must include page numbers for ease of reference during
the meeting.
• If attending electronically, ensure you have a computer with internet access to enable
you to participate electronically as an ‘Attendee’ to make your deputation/presentation
during the meeting. Please refer to following tutorial for ZOOM details:
https://support.zoom.us/hc/en-us/categories/200101697
Page 3 of 6
• If you do not have the necessary technology to participate by video, you may use a
telephone and call in to participate and make your deputation.
• If you are participating by telephone, you will not have the option to type in your name.
We will ask for the phone number you will be using to participate in the meeting. This
information will let us associate the correct name with your phone number. Please
note, that depending on volume, telephone numbers may be visible to the public;
however, every effort will be made to change prior to attendees being promoted to
panelist. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person to present a deputation.
• Once you have completed the Request for Public Participation Form for your
deputation and the zoom registration is closed, all applicants are uploaded to ZOOM.
Meeting invites are then sent by Zoom to the e-mail you provided in the registration
form.
• Please note this link is unique to you and should not be shared with others. Only those
whose registration form was received will be permitted attendance.
On the day of the meeting, we ask that you join the meeting fifteen to twenty (15 to 20)
minutes before your scheduled time. When joining, please type in your name so we
know who you are. You will be granted the ability to unmute your microphone when it
is your time to speak. Please wait for the Chair to request you to speak. You will be
able to hear and view the meeting in progress. You will not be able to see other
attendees nor will you appear on video.
• Please do not watch the livestream on YouTube while you are using the ZOOM
technology as this can distort the sound.
• If you have a presentation, it will be viewed through a shared screen and will be
controlled by the Township. During your presentation, we do ask that you state

• If your connection is lost and you are unable to reconnect within five minutes, the
deputation/ presentation will be deferred and the Clerk’s Department will contact you
to reschedule to another meeting date.
• Deputations and presentations will be recorded as part of the electronic meeting and
will be posted for public viewing on the Township of Oro-Medonte YouTube channel.
• Please contact the Clerk’s Department if you have any questions at yaubichon@oro-
medonte.ca prior to the meeting. Please note that this e-mail will not be responded to
once the meeting is in process; however, alternative e-mails will be provided.

As a municipality, we are committed to understanding the truth of our shared history, acknowledging our role in addressing the negative impacts that colonization continues to have on Indigenous Peoples, developing reciprocal relationships, and taking meaningful action toward reconciliation.

We are all Treaty people.

Motion for Which Notice was Previously Given by Councillor Farmer at the April 15, 2024 Regular Council meeting Re: Social Assistance Rates and Guaranteed Livable Income Program
This item has Video
 "WHEREAS the rising cost of living and rapid inflation are putting significant financial pressure on individuals and families, especially those living in poverty;

AND WHEREAS residents on programs such as Ontario Works receive maximum fixed monthly incomes of $733, and ODSP recipients receive $1,376;

AND WHEREAS people living with low income are more likely to be renters and the Community Foundation Focus on Housing report found that in 2021 more than 40% of homes in Owen Sound are rented;

AND WHEREAS rent is considered affordable when it is no more than 30% of gross annual income and the 2021 census reports that 38.3% of tenant households in Owen Sound are spending more than 30% of their income on housing;

AND WHEREAS as of March 31, 2024, there 1,650 Grey County households on the Community Housing Waitlist including only those who presently reside in the area;

AND WHEREAS the 2023 Grey County Housing Action Plan identified the need to advocate to the Provincial and Federal governments for housing solutions which may relate to “the ‘income’ side of the housing affordability equation, for example relating to minimum and living wages [and] social benefits (e.g., ODSP; OW)”;

AND WHEREAS poverty also increases food insecurity which negatively impacts physical and mental health especially for children and adequate income is an important social determinant of health that greatly impacts food security;

AND WHEREAS in 2023, the Salvation Army food bank use rose by 42% in Owen Sound and annual meals provided by OSHARE increased 18.6% or 23,000 meals from 2022;

AND WHEREAS in the 2024 Monitoring Food Affordability in Grey Bruce report on food insecurity, Grey Bruce Public Health calls on municipalities to “advocate for federal and provincial government policies (e.g.., increases to income tax credits for low-income households) and programs (e.g., basic income guarantee) to ensure an adequate and secure income for all in Canada”;

AND WHEREAS in February 2024 the Grey Bruce Poverty Task Force issued a call for income solutions to food insecurity;

AND WHEREAS neither municipal governments nor the non-profit sector have the resources to address the root causes of poverty on their own;

AND WHEREAS decreasing poverty levels benefits individuals and their communities by reducing reliance on food banks, social services, health care, emergency services, and other supports as well as improving quality of life and creating positive local economic impacts;

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT City Council join other municipalities across Ontario to urge the Federal and Provincial governments to increase social assistance rates for Ontario Works and the Ontario Disability Support Program and to establish a Guaranteed Livable Income program;

AND THAT this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, the Premier, the leaders of all parties sitting at Queen’s Park, the Minister of Children, Community and Social Services, the Minister of Health, the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, Alex Ruff, MP for Bruce-Grey-Owen Sound, and Rick Byers, MPP for Bruce-Grey-Owen Sound requesting a response;

AND FURTHER THAT this resolution also be shared with Grey County, Bruce County, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM), the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), and the Western Ontario Wardens’ Caucus (WOWC)."

Procedural Bylaw No. 4507(2022)
Being a bylaw to govern the proceedings of the Town of Pelham Council, its Committees, the conduct of its Members and the calling of Meetings.
Procedural By-law No. 4507(2022) was adopted on January 30, 2022, repealing and replacing Bylaw No. 4107(2019), as amended.
This By-law directs regular meetings of Council to be held on the first and third Wednesday of the month, commencing at 9:00 a.m. Public Meetings under the Planning Act are to be scheduled on the second Wednesday of the month, commencing at 5:30 p.m. Dates are subject to change to accommodate various Statutory Holidays, World Religious Holidays, major conferences and other known events. Please refer to the Council Meeting Schedule for approved meeting dates.
Additional notable changes include a new curfew of 1 pm, restructuring of regular meetings of Council to include Committee within Council, hybrid meeting participation, increase of three (3) to four (4) delegations permitted with a five (5) minute time limit, re-classification of Committees to include Statutory, Advisory and Volunteer Working Groups, a delegation submission deadline of ten (10) days prior to the meeting and the requirement to post agendas to the public five (5) days prior to the date of the meeting, being the Friday.

Delegation Request
In accordance with the Procedure By-law, Requests to Appear before Council shall be submitted in the prescribed form no later than 12:00 pm noon ten (10) days prior to the meeting. Delegations shall only be heard at regular meetings of Council. A maximum of four (4) delegations may be listed on the Agenda on a first-come, first-serve basis. Presentations are limited to 5 minutes.
Failure to provide the required information on time will result in a deferral or denial.

Council Correspondence 
The Town of Pelham's Council Correspondence Policy ensures that all written communication addressed to Council is managed effectively and respectfully. This policy covers all forms of correspondence received by the Town for Council’s attention, including petitions and requests for agenda inclusion.

Petitions Addressed to Council
Petitions addressed to Council shall be processed in accordance with the Town of Pelham Procedural By-law.  Petitions shall be legibly written or printed and shall not contain any obscene or improper material or language, and shall be signed by at least one (1) person, and filed with the Clerk. Petitions will be included on a public agenda including any personal, identifiable information. Sidewalk Market Zones and Storefront Cafe Seating
 Whereas the City of Peterborough's Central Area Urban Design Guidelines identify Market Zones as areas intended to support commercial spill-out, including sidewalk cafés, patios, signage and merchandise displays, and encourage these spaces as a means of animating the street and supporting an active downtown public realm;
And whereas small-scale café seating immediately adjacent to a storefront can contribute to downtown vitality and pedestrian activity while having minimal impact on the public right-of-way where an appropriate clear pedestrian path and accessibility requirements are maintained;
And whereas the City's current Outdoor Patio Program and licensing framework does not establish a separate category for low-impact storefront café seating and therefore generally subjects a small-scale arrangement, such as a table and a small number of chairs immediately adjacent to a storefront, to the same permitting framework as a larger outdoor patio;
And whereas a more proportionate approach to low-impact café seating may reduce unnecessary barriers for downtown businesses while continuing to protect accessibility, pedestrian movement, public safety and municipal operations;
Therefore be it resolved that:
Staff be directed to report back to Council with options to further support and implement the Sidewalk Market Zone objectives contained within the City's Central Area Urban Design Guidelines, including options for a simplified permitting or approval process for low-impact café seating located immediately adjacent to a storefront.
And further that the report consider how any recommended changes can support the City's broader objectives for downtown economic vitality, active storefronts, pedestrian-oriented streets and implementation of the Central Area Urban Design Guidelines while continuing to protect accessibility, public safety and municipal operations.
11.q

 Whereas Robert Winslow, founder of 4th Line Theatre, made an extraordinary contribution to the arts, culture and heritage of Peterborough and the surrounding region over more than three decades;
And whereas his work brought the stories and history of this region to life, created opportunities for generations of artists, and established a cultural institution with a lasting impact on our community;
Therefore be it resolved:
That staff report back on appropriate opportunities for the City of Peterborough to recognize and honour the life, work and legacy of Robert Winslow, in consultation with his family, 4th Line Theatre, and members of the local arts and cultural community.

1) PURPOSE:
The purpose of the report is to provide Council with information regarding a Zoning By-
law Amendment application initiated by Steven Rivers of South Coast Consultants on
behalf of the owner Hometown Properties Inc. for the property legally known as Lots 121
to 123 on Plan 12, and Part of Lots 368 and 369 on Plan 16, in the City of Port Colborne,
Regional Municipality of Niagara, municipally known as 168 and 176 Elm Street.
2) HISTORY, BACKGROUND, COUNCIL POLICY, PRACTICES
The application for Zoning By-law Amendment accompanied by a planning justification
report proposes to the zoning from I – Institutional and R4 – Fourth Density Residential
to R4-56, a special provision of the Fourth Density Residential zone that will allow for a
hall, apartment building and personal service business while recognizing the existing
location of the building, and allowing for a reduction in lot area per unit, minimum floor
area for a unit and parking. These changes are being sought to permit the conversion
from an institutional building into a 22-unit apartment building with a hall and office space
on the property.

The Notice of Public Meeting was circulated to required agencies, and property owners
within 120 metres of the property on November 24, 2020. Public notice signs were posted
on the property on or before November 24, 2020. Meeting details have been provided
along with the Council Agenda on the City’s website.

IMPLEMENTATION
1. Nyon acknowledges that it is responsible for implementing the recommendations that are
contained in the Risk Assessment Plan in order to mitigate risk, to improve safety, and to
prevent the unwanted release of hazardous materials.
2. Nyon acknowledges that it is responsible to implement the recommendations that are
contained in the Fire Emergency Plan in order to mitigate risk and respond to fire and other
emergencies on the Tank Farm Lands.

3. The parties acknowledge that the Safety Reports are living documents, and as the detailed
plans and engineered drawings are developed for the Tank Farm Lands, accordingly there
may be amendments to the Safety Reports, as appropriate.

4. Nyon acknowledges that it is wholly responsible for the cost of the implementation and the
ongoing performance of all recommendations contained in the Risk Assessment Plan
(collectively, the “Risk Assessment Plan Obligations”). The City shall not bear any of
the cost of risk mitigation set out in the Risk Assessment Plan. Nyon hereby indemnifies
and saves harmless the City, its employees, contractors and agents from any and all costs,
losses, actions and other liabilities that the City may incur in connection with, or resulting
from, Nyon’s failure to comply with or carry out the Risk Assessment Plan Obligations.
5. Nyon acknowledges that it is wholly responsible for the cost of the implementation and the
ongoing performance of all recommendations contained in the Fire Emergency Plan
(collectively, the “Fire Emergency Plan Obligations”). The City shall not bear any of the
cost of risk mitigation set out in the Fire Emergency Plan. Nyon hereby indemnifies and
saves harmless the City, its employees, contractors and agents from any and all costs,
losses, actions and other liabilities that the City may incur in connection with, or resulting
from, Nyon’s failure to comply with or carry out the Fire Emergency Plan Obligations.
6. Without limiting the obligations set out in paragraphs 4 and 5 above, Nyon agrees to pay
the training costs for municipal employees as required by the Safety Plans, currently
estimated to be $408,770, in accordance with the following schedule:
(a) $204,335 on application to the City for site plan approval; and
(b) $204,335 on application to the City for a building permit related to the Tank Farm
Lands.
7. Upon receipt of payment from Nyon, as stated in section 6 above, the City shall be
responsible for administering the training of municipal employees in accordance with the
Risk Assessment Plan and the Fire Emergency Plan.
DEFAULT
8. The occurrence of any one or more of the following events is an “Even of Default” within
the meaning of this Agreement:
(a) Nyon is not in compliance with the Risk Assessment Plan Obligations;
(b) Nyon is not in compliance with the Fire Emergency Plan Obligations;
(c) Nyon is not in compliance with any covenant, term or provision of this Agreement;

Upon the occurrence of an Event of Default, the City will provide written notice of the

in its entirety on or before the date which is five (5) days after the Default Notice has been
delivered to Nyon, then the City may, in addition to such other remedies as the City may
have under this Agreement, in law or otherwise, send a notice to Nyon ordering it to
immediately cease all operations on the Tank Farm Lands or to impose such other
restrictions and conditions on the use of the Tank Farm Lands as the City may, in its
absolute discretion, acting reasonably, impose for purposes of protection of the public (a
“Default Order”).

harm to the City that the City may not be adequately compensated for such damages by
monetary award alone. Accordingly, Nyon agrees that in the event of any such breach, and

available at law or otherwise.

10. Nyon acknowledges and agrees that the implementation, cost, and performance of the

owners of the land.

Agendas are typically posted approximately one week prior to each meeting. Minutes are posted after they have been reviewed and formally approved by Council.
Residents are encouraged to review agendas to stay informed about upcoming discussions and to read approved minutes for official records of Council decisions.
COUNCIL AGENDAS
Council agendas outline the items that will be discussed at upcoming meetings of Council. These documents provide an overview of reports, presentations, bylaws, and other matters requiring Council discussion or decision.
Agendas are typically posted approximately one week before each meeting to allow residents time to review upcoming municipal business.

MEETING MINUTES
Meeting minutes provide the official record of Council meetings. They summarize discussions, motions, resolutions, and decisions made by Council. Minutes are reviewed and approved at a subsequent Council meeting before being published as the official record.

THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER
BYLAW 13-2019
BEING A BYLAW TO APPOINT AN INTEGRITY COMMISSIONER
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, Chapter 25, Section 223.3 (1), authorizes the
municipality to appoint an Integrity Commissioner who reports to Council and who is
responsible for performing in an independent manner the functions assigned by the
municipality with respect to,
(a) the application of the code of conduct for members of Council and the code of conduct
for members of local boards or of either of them;
(b) the application of any procedures, rules and policies of the municipality and local boards
governing the ethical behaviour of members of council and of local boards or of either of
them.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION
OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER ENACTS AS FOLLOWING:
1) That Expertise for Municipalities (E4m) shall be appointed and act as Integrity
Commissioner.
2) That this appointment shall be subject to the executed Letter of Engagement,
attached as Appendix “A” of this Bylaw.
3) This Bylaw shall come into force and effect upon enactment.
4) This Bylaw may be cited as “Township of Schreiber Integrity Commissioner Bylaw
13-2019”.
Read a first and second time this 26th day of March, 2019.
Read a third time and finally enacted, this 26th day of March, 2019.

Whereas pursuant to Section 238 of the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended, every
municipality and local board shall pass a procedure By-law for governing the calling, place
and proceedings of meetings;
Now Therefore the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn Enacts as
follows;
Definitions
1. In this By-law:
a) “Abstain” means a member who is lawfully entitled to vote but chooses not to
exercise their right to vote on a matter, and in such cases in abstention shall be
deemed as a negative vote (Municipal Act S. 246. (2)).
b) “Clerk” means the Clerk of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
c) “Committee” means any advisory or other Committee, subcommittee or similar
entity of which at least 50 per cent of the members are also members of one or
more councils or local boards. A local board does not include police services
boards or public library boards (Municipal Act S. 238. (1)).
d) “Council” means the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
e) “Electronic Participation” includes telephone, video, audio or audio-visual conferencing,
or any other interactive method whereby Members, staff and the public are able to hear
the Member(s) participating by electronic means and the Member(s) participating by
electronic means are able to hear other Members, staff and the public.
f) “Head of Council” means the Mayor of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
g) “Live streaming” is a method of providing video over the internet in real time. The
video stream can be saved and archived allowing those with internet access the
ability to view recordings at their convenience.
h) “Meeting” means any regular, special, committee or other meeting of a Council, or
of a local board or of a committee of either of them, where,
(a) a quorum of members is present, and
(b) members discuss or otherwise deal with any matter in a way that materially
advanced the business or decision-making of the Council, local board or Committee
(Municipal Act S. 238 (1).
i) “Pecuniary Interest” means a direct or indirect pecuniary interest of a member of
Council within the meaning of the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act, R.S.O. 1990, as
amended.
j) “Presiding Officer” means the member of Council who, as determined under Section
12, 13 or 17 of this By-law, is responsible to preside over or act as the Chairperson
of a meeting.

REPORT
MEETING TYPE: Regular Council Meeting
To: Council
From: Jackie Trenholm, Deputy Clerk
Date: April 16, 2025
Subject: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
Report No.: 2025-529
TITLE: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
RECOMMENDATION:
THAT Council authorizes the passing of By-law No. 25-25, Being a By-law Relating to 2026
Municipal Election Matters (language(s) to be used for election forms/notices/information; use
of alternative voting method; use of vote-counting equipment).
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this recommendation is to enable Council to make certain decisions respecting
the 2026 Municipal Election, including the use of the "telephone/internet" voting method.
BACKGROUND:
Several items must be addressed relative to the 2026 Municipal Election, including:
1. Use of Alternative Voting Methods
2. Advance Poll
3. Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
4. Use of vote-counting equipment
5. Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
6. Payment of rebate for campaign contributions
7. Ward(s) review/changes
8. Electronic filing of financial statements
9. Submitting a By-law or question to the electors (question on the ballot)
10. Appointment of Compliance Committee
DISCUSSION:
Item No. 1: Use of Alternative Voting Methods
The Municipality had been employing the vote-by-mail (VBM) voting method for several prior
general municipal elections (2003, 2006, 2010 and 2014). This alternative voting method has
been successful, having yielded higher voter turnout rates over traditional elections in each of
the last four general elections.
While this method has increased voter turnout, compared to the traditional in-person polls, the
participation rate has decreased over the last decade-and-a-half, as follows:
• Voter turnout 2003 – 60.61%
• Voter turnout 2006 – 57.72%
• Voter turnout 2010 – 56.86%
• Voter turnout 2014 – 55.95%
Given this gradual, but steady, decline in voter participation, staff recommended the use of the
telephone/internet voting method in the 2018 general election, the 2020 by-election and the
2022 general election. Voter turnout for those elections was as follows:
• 2018 General Election – 55.21%
• 2020 By-election – 32.48%
• 2022 General Election - 33.10%
Given the trend in municipal elections, across Ontario, of having fewer voters participate in
such elections, achieving a 55.21% voter turnout in 2018 was excellent, and placed Sioux
Lookout in among the highest of voter turnout results in Ontario. By-elections typically result in
lower number of voters. The 2020 By-election turnout was approximately 2.5% higher than the
last by-election in 2015. The 2022 voter turnout was lower than the 2018 general election.
When there isn’t a mayoral race, voter turnout is typically lower.
Vote-by-Mail versus Telephone/Internet Voting – An Analysis
Election Principles
Despite which voting method is selected, it is the responsibility of the Clerk/Returning Officer
to uphold the following election principles:
• The secrecy and confidentiality of the individual votes is paramount;
• The election must be fair and non-biased;
• The election must be accessible to all voters;
• The integrity of the process must be maintained throughout the election;
• There must be certainty that the results of the election reflect the votes cast; and
• All voters and candidates must be treated fairly and consistently.
Vote by Mail – Overview
Electors receive a voting kit in the mail. They mail in their signed declaration form along with
their secrecy envelope containing their marked ballot. The declaration form is scanned prior to
voting day; the secrecy ballot is kept in a secure ballot box until the close of election. On
Election Day, Staff open the ballot boxes containing the secrecy envelopes and review each
ballot to determine if the ballot is spoiled or rejected. Staff then feed the ballots through a vote
tabulating machine or count them manually. Once all of the ballots have been fed through the
vote tabulator (or counted manually), the tabulator totals the votes and provides a printable
receipt of the results to election officials, or the totals of votes cast and counted manually are
reported to the Returning Officer.
Advantages and Disadvantages: Vote-by-mail (VBM)
Advantages:
Signed declaration – provides security against voter fraud
Improved size and efficiency. Desk top tabulators are hooked up to a PC laptop and can
scan 40 ballots per minute and results are quick. They also store the image of each
ballot for recount/audit purposes.
Longer voting period
Disadvantages:
With VBM, staff are required to facilitate vote tabulation by feeding ballots into vote
tabulators, or physically/manually examining each ballot, and must make a determination
with respect to spoiled and rejected ballots
Staff resources and time - secrecy ballot envelopes cannot be opened until close of
voting. Ballots must then be organized, reviewed, scanned, counted and then eventually
destroyed.
If not using vote-counting equipment, manual vote-counting is extremely time consuming
– unofficial results in 2014 were not available until 2:00 a.m. (6 hours after close of
voting).
Opportunity for Spoiled ballots – vote does not count (e.g. elector included ballot with
signed declaration card; no signed declaration form or no declaration form included;
marking on the ballot that does not indicate choice or there is no marking on ballot)
Spoiled ballots – the voter has no way of knowing if their ballot was spoiled. There is no
confirmation process.
Potential to receive voter kits by unintended recipient which includes the ballot
Postal service – takes five days for voter to receive vote by mail kit; takes five days for
municipal office to receive marked ballot with secrecy envelope (total 5-10 days) by mail,
unless dropped off at municipal office
Costs – more expensive voting method due to need for more staff; manual count;
training of staff, etc.
Internet/Telephone Voting - Overview
Internet Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They log onto the election server on any computer,
vote by using their keyboard in response to a virtual ballot, the vote is stored on the election
software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation number or
printable receipt. At the close of Election Day, the internet software totals the votes received
and provides a printable receipt of the results to election officials.
Telephone Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They call a toll-free number from a touchtone phone;
vote by pressing buttons in response to a voice recording and the vote is stored by the
election software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation
number. At the close of Election Day, the telephone voting results are combined with the
internet voting results for one total result. A printable receipt of the results is made available to
election officials.
It is recommended that both internet and telephone options be provided to electors for the
2026 municipal election.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Internet/Telephone Voting
Advantages:
Less staff and administrative resources required and less expensive overall (except in
first year of implementation, due to public education costs)
No ballot errors/spoiled ballots because the software does not permit it. There are built in
reminders or safeguards to prevent accidental voting
Voter is provided with confirmation that their vote counted by issuance or confirmation of
a receipt
Elector participation is real time and results are immediate
Ballot destruction after election is electronically completed and verified
Voter has the opportunity to review selection and make changes prior to submitting vote
Lowered carbon footprint; environmentally sustainable due to less paper required
Recounts are instantaneous and inexpensive
Most accessible form of voting. Allows persons with disabilities the opportunity to
completely mark their ballot in private without the assistance of a designated friend or
election official, therefore providing greater dignity
Disadvantages:
Not everyone has access to a computer or is computer literate; however, telephone
voting would be the alternative to those who do not have internet access or low levels of
computer literacy
Security and viruses; voter authentication - however, the preferred vendor has
implemented robust measures to mitigate such threats
Telephone voting takes time – audio ballot
Telephone voting - Voter cannot see the names of the candidates
Other Benefits of Internet/telephone Voting
• provides convenience, accommodates changing lifestyles, demanding work schedules;
• enhances accessibility for students studying away from home, those travelling, shift
workers, infirmed persons, and persons with language barriers.
• for persons with disabilities, it provides greater dignity and privacy for electors;
• engages a wider range of age demographics, provides greater accuracy and fast results, is
convenient for seasonal residents, and has the potential for increased voter turnout.
Public Education & Outreach
Public education and outreach will play a critical role in the 2026 municipal election, should the
telephone/internet voting method be adopted. Although this method has been used several
times in Sioux Lookout, to ensure that concerns and questions regarding this voting method
are adequately addressed, a prior election education campaigns will be enhanced and
administered by the Clerk.
In order to mitigate concerns regarding accessibility for senior citizens to vote, the Clerk, as in
the 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections, will arrange to attend multi-residential senior complexes
throughout the community to provide senior citizens the opportunity to vote at their residence.
Additionally, for those who are not comfortable with internet voting or telephone voting on their
own, an electronic voting station will be established at the Municipal Office, with staff on hand
to provide assistance, as requested. Furthermore, remote voting locations will be established
at the Sioux Lookout Senior’s Centre, the Sioux Lookout Meno Ya Win Health Centre, the
William George Extended Care Unit, the Nishnawbe-Gamik Friendship Centre, and in Hudson.
Accessibility for Persons with Disabilities
Internet/Telephone voting offers the most accessible form of voting. Voters are offered the
greatest secrecy and less assisted voting thereby enhancing the quality of the vote and
anonymity.
Security
Section 89 of the Municipal Elections Act provides for penalties for any contravention of the
Act, as follows:
A person is guilty of an offence if he or she,
(a) votes without being entitled to do so;
(b) votes more times than this Act allows;
(c) votes in a voting place in which he or she is not entitled to vote;
(d) induces or procures a person to vote when that person is not entitled to do so;
(e) having appointed a voting proxy that remains in force, votes otherwise than by the proxy;
(f) having been appointed a voting proxy, votes under the authority of the proxy when the
elector has cancelled the proxy, is no longer entitled to vote or has died;
(g) before or during an election, publishes a false statement of a candidate’s withdrawal;
(h) furnishes false or misleading information to a person whom this Act authorizes to obtain
information;
(i) without authority, supplies a ballot to anyone;
(j) delivers to the deputy returning officer to be placed in a ballot box a paper other than the
ballot the deputy returning officer gave him or her;
(k) takes a ballot away from the voting place;
(l) at an election, takes, opens or otherwise deals with a ballot, a ballot box, or a book or
package of ballots without having authority to do so;
(m) attempts to do something described in clauses (a) to (l)
Clearly, accountability of voting rests with the voter and there are penalties associated with
voter fraud. Unsupervised voting facilitates the potentiality of these offences. Voter
impersonation, coercion and fraud are concerns which are mitigated through the design of any
voting system, regardless of whether it is a supervised or unsupervised model.
Item No. 2: Advance Poll
The use of the vote-by-mail or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for
advance polls. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk,
via the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 3: Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
The vote-by-mail voting or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for these
measures. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk, via
the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 4: Use of Vote-Counting Equipment
The Municipality had used Electronic Vote Tabulators (EVTs) in the 2000, 2003, 2006 and
2010 Municipal Elections. Ballots were created and coded by Ward, School Board
candidate(s) and Municipal Council (Mayor and Councillors-at-Large) candidates and
processed by the EVT on voting day. In the past, this has resulted in election results within
minutes of the close of polls.
For the 2014 Municipal Election, the Clerk chose to use manual vote-counting procedures
given that vote-counting equipment rental had significantly increased in cost increase since
the 2010 Municipal Election. The primary impact on the election was a longer time-frame
between the close of polls and the announcement of the unofficial results – a total of six hours.
If Council chooses to use the Vote-by-Mail voting method in 2026, vote tabulators will be
required to ensure the efficient tabulation of results; this is an additional cost to using this
voting method.
Item No. 5: Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
Prescribed forms (those set by legislation) must be provided in English only, but may be
provided in English and French only. Other forms/notices/information can be provided in
English, French or any other language, providing Council passes a by-law permitting such.
In one previous election, prior to 2003, some of the Notices were provided in both English and
Oji-Cree. This exercise was costly and was subsequently discontinued. It should be noted that
the onus is on the elector to provide translation services when voting. In 2003, 2006 and 2010,

Subject: August Concert Series Bluewater Park
Recommendation:
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater
Park Bandshell for the month of August;
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities.
Background:
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage.
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert.
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events,
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy.
The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit
events.
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula.
Staff are also seeking sponsorship for the Thursday night music series and if successful, the
initiative will be partially/fully funded via sponsorship. At the Time of writing this report,
sponsorship funding has not been secured, hence the request to utilize MAT funds. Any
sponsorship funding will be utilized to pay for the concert series and replenish MAT
reserves, if funding comes at a later date.
Options:
A $5,000 to be allocated from the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve for the
Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater Park Bandshell in the month of
August.

The Manager of Economic Development will work with the Recreation and Parks
Department on venue booking and equipment set up. Communications of the concert series
will be through the website and social media channels.

Day event.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 1: Transparent and Accountable Governance, Goal

Background: The Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) was adopted by Council
in 2021 as a means to streamline the requests that Council receives from members of
the community seeking funding. The policy has undergone amendments since its initial
adoption with the last amendment being adopted in 2024. One of the requirements in
the policy is that the grant recipients are required to make a final report 90 days
following their event or by November 30, 2024, whichever is earlier.
The 2024 program application period closed on November 30, 2023 with eighteen (18)
submissions being received. Two of the applicants did not receive funding as they did not
meet the program criteria, proposing projects for Town and other Government Agency
property. Subsequent to deliberations, Council adopted resolution R-07-2024 wherein
funding awards were decided and additionally, Council decided to remove the previous
"automatically recurring" grants which staff had been including in the annual budgets. Using
the last remaining budget allocation, Council has also provided funding support to two
additional organizations since the original allocation of funding.
Staff have received the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club which supported
the annual Canada Day event held in Bluewater Park. The grant allocation was $500.
The final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club explains that the event had vendors,
a BBQ, a pancake breakfast and family entertainment. The Wiarton District Optimist Club
was fortunate in that they secured several local sponsors and funding through the Celebrate
Canada Grant Program. All of the funds, including those from the Town allowed them to
hold a family friendly event which they feel was a success. The Optimist Club was able to
finish the event with a surplus of $2,839.08. The Town's donation was directed toward the
Bluewater Park rental costs.
Options:
a) Receive the final report, as presented.
b) Seek additional information from the Wiarton District Optimist Club.

Community Grant Program
1.0 Purpose
The Town of South Bruce Peninsula has established the Community Grant Program to:
• Improve the well-being of individuals, neighbourhoods and the municipality as
a whole by directing Community Grant funding to eligible recipients who can
demonstrate the greatest need in the community while supporting Council's
strategic priorities.
• Diversify the availability of activities available to all residents of our
community and contribute to enhancing the quality of life.
• Through this support, it is hoped that other funding may be leveraged, and
participants and volunteers can be supported, attracted and retained.
• Ensure that the process to review and allocate Community Grant funding is
transparent, consistent and achieves the optimal impact for the investment
provided.
2.0 Authority
This policy is established pursuant to Section 107 of the Municipal Act, 2001 which
allows a municipality, subject to Section 106, to make grants, on such terms as to
security and otherwise as the Council considers appropriate, to any person, group or
body, including a fund, within or outside the boundaries of the municipality for any
purpose that Council considers to be in the interests of the municipality.
3.0 Budget
On an annual basis, Council will determine the total funding envelope for Community
Grants as part of the annual operating budget.
As the number of grant requests may exceed funds available and budget priorities may
change from year to year, applicants are not guaranteed funding. A Community Grant
approved in any year is not considered a commitment by the Town to continue financial
assistance in future years.

The Community Grant Program will provide grants to support eligible community-based
organizations for community-based activities.
Applications must align with one or more of the Town's strategic priorities.
An activity funded by a Community Grant must be open to the public at minimal or no
charge and must be accessible to all community members by satisfying the
requirements of the Ontario Human Rights Code, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms,
and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act.
The Community Grant Program is intended to provide funding that is supplemental to
the overall financial requirements to carry on a planned activity. The Community Grant
Program is not intended to be the sole source of funding for an activity.
Eligible applicants are also encouraged to seek funding from other sources, including
fundraising, sponsorships, donations, and/or Federal/Provincial grant programs.
Applicants who have, or will have, funding from alternate sources must disclose this
funding as a part of the budget submitted in support of the Community Grant Program
Application. If no other sources of funding have been pursued, applicants are required
to provide information on the reasons why other opportunities were not explored.
Applicants seeking up to a maximum of $500 are not required to submit a budget with
their application. Any applicant seeking between $500 - $5,000 must provide a budget
with their application to clearly show how Community Grant funds will be used.
A successful recipient of the Community Grant program may receive a cash Grant of up
to $5,000 for the activity. As a guide, Council will normally only provide Grant funds up
to 25% of the project budget, or $5,000, whichever is the lesser amount. For projects
where there is a demonstrated significant, unique, or exceptional financial need, and
where 25% of the project budget is less than $5,000, Council may waive the 25%
granting cap and approve Grant funds up to $5,000.
Through the Community Grant Program, Council may approve the provision of "in-kind"
fee-waivers to a maximum of $2,000 per applicant. For clarification, building and
planning fees are not eligible to be waived under the Community Grant Program.

• Donations to third-parties and charitable organizations.
• Increasing endowment funds.
• Funding requests of more than $5,000 per organization in any single Grant cycle.

8.0 Application Process
Information relevant to the Grants process including application due dates and
guidelines to apply will be advertised in local media and on the Town website at
www.southbrucepeninsula.com
The funding call will occur once per year, usually commencing in the month of
September. Grants awarded will cover the period January - December of the following
year.
All organizations must complete the application form in full which means that each
question must be answered and all the requested supporting documentation must be
submitted. Incomplete applications may not be considered. The Town reserves the right
to contact any organization for information which requires clarification.
Applications must be received by the Town on or before 4:00 pm on the advertised
submission deadline. No late applications will be considered. It is the sole responsibility
of the applicant to ensure that the Town receives completed applications.
Eligible organizations can submit only one (1) application per year.
Requests for in-kind grants such as waiving of Town fees or use of municipal facilities
should be accompanied with a dollar value estimate that has been confirmed with the
applicable Town Department.

9.0 Evaluation of Applications
The Town operating budget will be approved with a funding envelope for Community
Grants.
The evaluation of applications can take place after budget approval. It is not necessary
to have the allocations to specific Grant recipients included in the Town budget.
Eligible applications will be evaluated based on the following criteria:
• How the activity will support the Town's strategic priorities;
• Contribution to the community and impact to residents of the Town by
strengthening our community and growing our economy;
• Evidence of support from other partners, volunteers and other sources of
funding to enable the organization or activity to be sustainable;
• Additional financial and non-financial resources being leveraged from other
sources;
• Evidence that the organization needs the funding. Organizations that have
budgets or financial statements indicating reserves or a surplus will be
required to provide explanations of the surplus and how the organization
intends to use it;
• Sound organizational track record. This considers if the organization has the
ability, skills and capacity to undertake the activity;
• That the activities do not unnecessarily duplicate successful efforts that
already exist in the community;
• Sustainability of the organization and activity as applicable; and
• The amount of funding requested by applicants and the funding available in
the program.
All applicants will receive notification of Council's decision of whether or not their
application was successful.

Recommendation:
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater
Park Bandshell for the month of August;
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities.
Background:
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage.
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert.
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events,
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy.
The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit
events.
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula.
Staff are also seeking sponsorship for the Thursday night music series and if successful, the
initiative will be partially/fully funded via sponsorship. At the Time of writing this report,
sponsorship funding has not been secured, hence the request to utilize MAT funds. Any
sponsorship funding will be utilized to pay for the concert series and replenish MAT
reserves, if funding comes at a later date.

Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater Park Bandshell in the month of
August.

Subject: Wiarton District Optimist Club Community Grant Program Final Report -

Recommendation: That Council receives the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist
Club as it relates to the Community Grant Program allocation to support the Wiarton Canada
Day event.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 1: Transparent and Accountable Governance, Goal
3: Collaboration and Partnerships and Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
would be the general links to the Strategic Plan.
Specific Objectives and Actions would be:
3.1 Maximize Shared Services and Resources
3.1.1 Explore formal and informal opportunities to collaborate for expanded service
delivery, reduced cost and improved community benefit
Background: The Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) was adopted by Council
in 2021 as a means to streamline the requests that Council receives from members of
the community seeking funding. The policy has undergone amendments since its initial
adoption with the last amendment being adopted in 2024. One of the requirements in
the policy is that the grant recipients are required to make a final report 90 days
following their event or by November 30, 2024, whichever is earlier.
The 2024 program application period closed on November 30, 2023 with eighteen (18)
submissions being received. Two of the applicants did not receive funding as they did not
meet the program criteria, proposing projects for Town and other Government Agency
property. Subsequent to deliberations, Council adopted resolution R-07-2024 wherein
funding awards were decided and additionally, Council decided to remove the previous
"automatically recurring" grants which staff had been including in the annual budgets. Using
the last remaining budget allocation, Council has also provided funding support to two
additional organizations since the original allocation of funding.
Staff have received the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club which supported
the annual Canada Day event held in Bluewater Park. The grant allocation was $500.
The final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club explains that the event had vendors,
a BBQ, a pancake breakfast and family entertainment. The Wiarton District Optimist Club
was fortunate in that they secured several local sponsors and funding through the Celebrate
Canada Grant Program. All of the funds, including those from the Town allowed them to
hold a family friendly event which they feel was a success. The Optimist Club was able to
finish the event with a surplus of $2,839.08. The Town's donation was directed toward the
Bluewater Park rental costs.
Options:
a) Receive the final report, as presented.
b) Seek additional information from the Wiarton District Optimist Club.
